target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is educationally valuable because it develops fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and science interest.
objection: AG2 argues that dissection is not required for biology learning or standards, and that synthetic models, computer simulations, and virtual labs can teach the same anatomical concepts effectively without using animals, so the claimed educational necessity is unnecessary.

target: AG1’s ethical claim that dissection is a productive use of animals already dead and therefore does not require taking new animals.
objection: AG2 counters that the real-world supply chain for dissection animals is largely driven by wild capture, which is inhumane, reduces local populations, and decreases biodiversity; therefore the ethical mitigation claim is misleading.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can teach the same content and make real-animal dissection educationally unnecessary.
objection: AG1 responds that alternatives do not provide the same learning experience because real dissection uniquely offers tactile three-dimensional anatomical inspection, hands-on tool use that builds fine motor and hand-eye coordination, and critical-thinking work from direct observation.

target: AG2’s claim that most dissection animals come from wild capture and that this makes the practice ethically unacceptable.
objection: AG1 disputes the premise that dissection sourcing is mainly wild-caught, arguing that in typical classroom use the animals are already dead byproducts, such as fetal pigs from the meat industry, so wild-capture harms are not the primary driver.

target: AG1’s claim that over 98% of dissected animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are harmless byproducts destined for disposal.
objection: AG2 says that even if some animals are byproducts, dissection still depends on a supply chain that largely uses wild-captured animals, so the idea that the practice mainly uses already-dead animals and avoids serious welfare harm is not accurate.

target: AG2’s claim that wild capture is the dominant source of dissection animals and that this defeats the ethical mitigation argument.
objection: AG1 says AG2 has not established that claim and reiterates that classroom dissection usually uses already-dead specimens and meat-industry byproducts, so the alleged wild-capture harm does not undercut the central ethical mitigation.

target: AG2’s implication that any non-byproduct sourcing eliminates the ethical mitigation claimed for dissection.
objection: AG1 argues that the ethical question is whether classroom dissection requires killing animals specifically for dissection, and that a majority-based mitigation still matters even if not every specimen comes from a harmless source; thus the presence of some non-ideal sourcing does not erase the reduced incremental harm.

target: AG2’s objection that byproduct status does not remove the ethical concern because some specimens may still be sourced in ways that are not harmless.
objection: AG1 says the relevant point is that standard classroom specimens, especially fetal pigs, come from the meat industry as byproducts and would otherwise be discarded, so schools are using existing carcasses rather than creating a need for new animal deaths.

target: AG1’s claim that using fetal pigs and other byproducts means classroom dissection does not create new animal deaths.
objection: AG2 argues that repurposing killed animals does not eliminate the moral problem of killing, and that byproduct demand can still sustain or expand slaughter, so the claim that dissection adds no new animal harm is not substantiated.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is not necessary for medical or physician training.
objection: AG1 replies that the relevant educational value is not physician training alone: school biology aims to build foundational understanding, practical skills, and scientific interest, all of which real dissection can support through hands-on experience and memorable “aha” moments.

target: AG1’s claim that models and simulations cannot fully replicate the unique learning experience of real dissection.
objection: AG2 says the main educational goals—learning anatomy, interpreting structures, and practicing careful observation—can be met with synthetic models, computer simulations, virtual labs, and other non-animal materials, so real animal tissue is not uniquely necessary.

target: AG2’s repeated claim that medical-training requirements are the relevant standard for evaluating school dissection.
objection: AG1 says that is the wrong standard because school biology is about foundational understanding and scientific aptitude, not just medical training, and that real dissection offers direct tactile and visual learning plus career motivation that alternatives do not fully replicate.

target: AG1’s assumption that models and virtual labs cannot reproduce the learning value of manipulating real tissue.
objection: AG2 argues that the learning benefits attributed to dissection depend on generic task features—using tools, locating structures, and interpreting anatomy—not on the specimen being a dead animal, so comparable alternatives can reproduce the relevant learning mechanisms.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can fully match the learning value of real dissection.
objection: AG1 counters that real dissection still offers concrete hands-on examination of real anatomy, building practical skills and critical thinking from direct tactile and visual evidence, and that alternatives do not fully replicate this experience.

target: AG1’s claim that models and virtual labs do not fully replicate the meaningful learning from dissecting real animals.
objection: AG2 says the learning gains are not unique to real animals because synthetic models and simulations can teach the same anatomy and allow students to practice procedures repeatedly, while avoiding specimen variability and one-time-use limitations.

target: AG1’s ethics argument that dissection mostly avoids new animal killing because the specimens are already dead or are byproducts.
objection: AG2 argues that procurement creates ongoing demand and, in practice, much dissection supply is obtained through wild capture, so the activity still depends on harmful sourcing and is not ethically insulated merely because some specimens are byproducts.
